Editor’s note: The previous article, 160,000 speakers? The secret sonic weapon behind the Las Vegas Sphere, part 1, explained why sound design inside the giant Sphere is so hard. Now let’s see how the problems were overcome!

The secret weapon: Holoplot X1 and wave field synthesis

Taken together, the difficulties of sound control in the Sphere described in part 1 call for a system that can freely steer the direction of sound beams and shape their coverage, and that can also deliver multichannel surround or other immersive audio. The solution is the X1, a scalable Matrix Array loudspeaker system developed by Holoplot in Berlin, which achieves software-controlled beam steering based on wave field synthesis (WFS). Wave field synthesis is a technique for reconstructing the spatial position of sound sources. It rests on the Huygens–Fresnel principle: by setting the phase, delay and gain of many drivers, it forms many small wavefronts that add up to a single, coherent sound field, so that listeners localize sound somewhere other than at the loudspeakers themselves. The image below shows a single X1-MD96 module, made up of 96 high- and low-frequency drivers. Each driver has its own signal processing channel, and an embedded system at the back of the loudspeaker supplies the processing parameters needed to form the wave-field-synthesis beams.

Image: holoplot.com. X1-MD96 module

The technology does not only let you control where a sound source seems to be. It also means the system can control what should be heard at a given point in space, for example the position of one listener’s ear. Extend that single point to many points, and you can control the result over a surface or a whole area. This is one of the keys to how the system achieves sound control.

Image: holoplot.com. Recreating the spatial position of a virtual point source

Building on this, stacking loudspeaker modules horizontally and vertically into a matrix makes the system scalable and lets it control areas of different shapes and sizes precisely, as needed. As the image below shows, a matrix formed from a group of modules can deliver highly uniform sound pressure across an area.

Image: holoplot.com. Area coverage from a matrix array

1. An acoustically transparent screen with loudspeakers behind it

This software-defined beam control is the key to solving the Sphere’s acoustic problems. It means the loudspeakers can be placed behind the screen, with software then taking care of coverage and sound quality for multiple audience zones. The Sphere’s LED screen is made up of about 64,000 panels, and what makes them special is that they are acoustically transparent.

The image below shows the coverage design of the Sphere’s sound system. Besides a main array behind the stage (the proscenium array), many smaller X1 arrays are placed all around the sphere. All these modules are hidden behind the screen, so they do not spoil the view.

Image: holoplot.com. Design of the Sphere’s X1 coverage system

2. Several kinds of beam control

X1 uses three different beam algorithms for coverage and optimization:

– Coverage Beam

You define the shape of the area to be covered in software, and the algorithm computes the signal processing parameters each driver needs to optimize the result for that area.

The image below shows Holoplot’s system design software, Plan. The venue is divided into several target zones following the actual seating, and the colors show the sound pressure level (SPL) distribution obtained from acoustic simulation. Optimizing for a zone also means attenuating the energy outside it, and this attenuation greatly reduces reflections from the building’s surfaces, which improves clarity.

It is also worth mentioning that feeding several zones independently opens up some interesting applications. A venue could, for example, be divided into zones by language, so that at the same moment audience members with different language preferences experience a film or event in their own language.

– Parametric Beams

These are closer to the directional beams of conventional line arrays: the beam’s direction (vertical and horizontal steering angles) and width (opening angle) can be defined in software. Because they are lighter and easier to compute, each array group can generate more of them at once.

– Virtual Source

A virtual point source can be placed anywhere in space, which enables object-based spatial audio. It opens up truly immersive listening for many kinds of immersive experience.

Image: avinteractive.com. A forest expedition experience at an Illuminarium venue, with spatial audio from Holoplot X1

3. Solving the sweet-spot problem in large venues

With conventional 7.1 or 5.1 surround, once a venue gets large, everyone outside the central area misses out on true surround or hears obvious channel distortion. Wave field synthesis can divide a large venue into many small coverage zones, each precisely tuned in delay, phase and EQ, so that everyone gets a sweet spot.

How to handle so many signals

Sound design for Sphere shows is extremely complex too, generating hundreds or even thousands of independent audio channels. How can they all be transported reliably? With conventional analog or point-to-point digital transmission, the amount of cabling would be enormous and delay compensation laborious, bringing high maintenance costs and making troubleshooting extremely hard.

To solve these problems, the Sphere and Holoplot adopted the AES67/Ravenna protocols, based on open AoIP (audio over IP). This is a way of transporting media over the Internet Protocol: by packing audio signals and the information that goes with them into network packets, many channels can be sent in real time over Ethernet with ultra-low latency. By defining audio parameters such as bit rate and sample rate, and using PTP (Precision Time Protocol) for high-precision clock synchronization together with multicast, hundreds of audio channels can be distributed in real time, with extremely low latency, over a single RJ45 network cable and a switch.

Another big advantage of networked audio is that redundancy is easy to achieve efficiently. One relatively simple arrangement is to set up a complete second LAN for backup audio. Under software control, if a fault occurs during a show, the system can quickly switch to the backup path, and the show goes on.

Conclusion

By combining a spherical building with a vast LED screen, the Sphere posed unique challenges for its sound system:

  • How can the loudspeakers “disappear” from view?

  • How can reflections and focusing inside a sphere be overcome?

  • How can every tier of the audience get a consistent listening experience?

  • How can immersive 3D sound be delivered in a space for 20,000 people?

Holoplot’s beam-synthesis approach, combined with networked-audio standards, met these demanding coverage requirements and opened up further possibilities for artistic innovation. Beyond conventional surround, Dolby Atmos and object-based audio, it allows interesting experiments such as multilingual audio and different content in different zones. Since the main aim of this article is to introduce the basic requirements of sound control, I will not go through those other applications and technologies here.

For interested readers, I recommend an article on how U2’s FOH engineer Joe O’Herlihy and producer Steve Lillywhite used the system for a more artistic mix design, for example sending the effects channels of The Edge’s guitar up into the dome and using the building’s natural reflections to create a grander sound. See “Mixing U2’s Mighty Sound for the Sphere”: https://www.mixonline.com/live-sound/venues/mixing-u2s-mighty-sound-within-the-sphere.

Dig a little deeper and there are many other challenges too, such as wavelength-dependent differences in directivity across frequency bands, how system redundancy is implemented in practice, how such massive signal processing is realized, and downmixes for third-party sound systems (such as those in the VIP suites). I won’t go through them one by one here either.

This year the Backstreet Boys are coming to the Sphere as well. For countless of us born in the ’70s, ’80s and ’90s, they were among our first musical loves. To everyone lucky enough to see them there: enjoy your walk down memory lane.

About the author: Jiajun Yang holds a PhD in music technology from the University of York in the UK. He went on to a postdoc in sonification with the Ambient Intelligence group at Bielefeld University in Germany, and joined Holoplot’s software team in 2020. He loves programming and audio technology, knows AES67 and Dante networked audio well, and has lately followed the crowd down the Rust rabbit hole.
